tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Valence electrons are the outermost electrons of an atom that participate in chemical bonding. The number of valence electrons determines how many bonds an atom can form.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap the electron dots around the carbon atom to count its 4 valence electrons.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Most atoms are stable when surrounded by 8 electrons in their outer shell. Covalent bonds form by sharing electron pairs to satisfy this rule.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Drag lone pairs from oxygen to complete the octet on the highlighted atom.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Lone pairs are pairs of valence electrons not involved in bonding. They are crucial for nucleophilicity and contribute to molecular geometry.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Identify and tap all lone pairs on the nitrogen atom in the molecule shown.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Electronegativity is an atom's ability to attract shared electrons toward itself. Fluorine is the most electronegative element; cesium is the least.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Drag the electronegativity slider to rank C, N, O, and F from lowest to highest.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: When two atoms of different electronegativity share a bond, the electrons shift toward the more electronegative atom, creating a polar bond with δ+ and δ− ends.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap the atom that carries the δ− partial charge in the C–O bond shown.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: A dipole moment is a vector quantity measuring the overall charge separation in a molecule. Symmetrical molecules can have polar bonds but zero net dipole.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Rotate the 3D molecule until the net dipole arrow points away from you, then tap Confirm.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Resonance describes molecules that cannot be represented by a single Lewis structure. The true structure is a hybrid — a blend of all valid contributors.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Swipe right to draw the second resonance contributor for the carboxylate anion.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Delocalization spreads electron density over multiple atoms, lowering potential energy and increasing stability. Benzene is the classic example.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap each bond in benzene that participates in the delocalized π system.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Formal charge = valence electrons − lone pair electrons − ½ bonding electrons. The best resonance structure minimizes formal charges.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Calculate and enter the formal charge on nitrogen in the nitro group shown.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: A nucleophile is an electron-rich species that donates electrons to form a new bond. Common nucleophiles include OH⁻, CN⁻, and NH₃.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap all the nucleophiles from the list: OH⁻, H₂, BF₃, CN⁻, AlCl₃, Br⁻.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: An electrophile is an electron-deficient species that accepts electrons to form a new bond. Carbocations, H⁺, and Lewis acids are all electrophiles.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Drag the arrow from the nucleophile lone pair to the electrophilic carbon shown.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Nucleophilicity is kinetic (attack speed), while basicity is thermodynamic (affinity for H⁺). A species can be nucleophilic but weakly basic, or vice versa.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Sort these four species by nucleophilicity in polar aprotic solvent: F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: A functional group is a specific arrangement of atoms that determines a molecule's reactivity. The rest of the molecule (the 'R group') is mostly inert.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap and label the three functional groups visible on the amino acid structure.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: The carbonyl (C=O) is the most important functional group in organic chemistry. Aldehydes, ketones, esters, and carboxylic acids all contain a carbonyl.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Circle the carbonyl carbon in each of the four molecules shown — which is most electrophilic?

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: IUPAC nomenclature prioritizes functional groups: carboxylic acid > ester > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene > alkyne.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Drag the functional group names onto the correct atoms of the displayed compound.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: A curved arrow shows the movement of a pair of electrons from a source (tail) to a destination (head). The tail always starts on an electron pair or bond.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Draw a curved arrow from the lone pair on oxygen to the electrophilic carbon — tap tail, then tap head.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: When an arrow starts on a bond, it shows that bond breaking. The electrons move toward the arrow's head, generating either a radical or an ionic intermediate.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Draw the heterolytic cleavage arrow that breaks the C–Br bond, sending both electrons to bromine.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Arrows always flow from electron-rich to electron-poor regions. Never draw an arrow backward (from positive to negative). Each step must be electronically balanced.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Identify the one incorrect arrow in the mechanism shown and tap it to flag the error.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: A carbocation is a carbon atom bearing only six electrons and a positive charge. Its stability increases with substitution: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Rank these four carbocations from most to least stable by dragging them into order.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Hyperconjugation is the delocalization of C–H σ-bond electrons into an adjacent empty p orbital. More C–H bonds adjacent to the cation means greater stabilization.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap all C–H bonds that are hyperconjugating with the carbocation center shown.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Carbocations rearrange via 1,2-hydride or 1,2-methyl shifts to form a more stable cation. This can change the carbon skeleton and give unexpected products.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Draw the 1,2-hydride shift arrow on the secondary carbocation to produce the tertiary cation.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: SN2 is a one-step substitution: the nucleophile attacks the back face of the electrophilic carbon while the leaving group departs simultaneously, causing inversion.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Drag the hydroxide ion to the correct face of CH₃Br to initiate the SN2 backside attack.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: SN1 is a two-step process: first the leaving group departs to form a planar carbocation, then the nucleophile attacks from either face, giving racemisation.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap the correct intermediate formed after Br⁻ departs from (CH₃)₃CBr in step 1 of SN1.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Bulky groups around the electrophilic carbon block the backside attack required for SN2. Tertiary substrates cannot undergo SN2 — they exclusively follow SN1.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap the carbon atom with the most bulky groups attached — this one will resist SN2.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: E2 is a one-step elimination: a base abstracts a β-hydrogen while the leaving group departs simultaneously, forming a π bond. The H and LG must be anti-periplanar.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Rotate the Newman projection until the H and Br are anti-periplanar, then tap 'Eliminate'.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Under E2 conditions with a non-bulky base, the more substituted (more stable) alkene is the major product — this is Saytzeff's (Zaitsev's) rule.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Select the Saytzeff product from the two possible alkenes formed from 2-bromobutane.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Substitution and elimination compete. High temperature, strong bulky base, and tertiary substrate favour elimination. Weak nucleophile and primary substrate favour substitution.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Given the reagent conditions shown, drag the arrow to either the SN2 or E2 pathway.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: A stereocentre (chiral centre) is an atom — usually carbon — bonded to four different groups. Its mirror image is non-superimposable, giving two enantiomers.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap every stereocentre in the displayed molecule. There may be more than one.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Assign R or S by ranking substituents 1–4 by CIP priority, then trace 1→2→3. Clockwise = R (Rectus); counter-clockwise = S (Sinister). Swap if group 4 faces you.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Drag the priority labels (1–4) onto the correct substituents, then tap R or S.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images (all stereocentres inverted). Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images — some centres are the same, some differ.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: From the four structures shown, tap the one that is the enantiomer of the reference molecule.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: In HX addition to an asymmetric alkene, H⁺ adds to the carbon with more hydrogens (forming the more stable carbocation), and X⁻ adds to the other carbon.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap the carbon that will receive the Br in Markovnikov addition of HBr to propene.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Addition of Br₂ to an alkene proceeds through a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate. Br⁻ then attacks the back face, giving anti addition of two bromine atoms.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Draw the bromonium ion intermediate by dragging Br₂ onto the double bond of cyclohexene.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Anti addition means the two new groups add to opposite faces of the double bond. Br₂ addition to cyclic alkenes always gives trans (anti) dihalides.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Select the correct stereochemical product of Br₂ addition to cyclohexene — trans or cis?

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: EAS proceeds via a resonance-stabilized arenium ion (Wheland intermediate) formed when the electrophile attacks the aromatic π system. A proton is then lost to restore aromaticity.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Draw the arenium ion formed when NO₂⁺ attacks benzene — drag arrows to show the three resonance forms.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Electron-donating groups (–OH, –NH₂, –alkyl) activate the ring and direct electrophiles to ortho and para positions by stabilizing the arenium ion at those sites.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap all positions on toluene where an incoming electrophile would preferentially attack.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Electron-withdrawing groups (–NO₂, –C≡N, –COOH) deactivate the ring and direct electrophiles to the meta position because o/p arenium ions are extra-destabilized.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Given nitrobenzene, drag the incoming Br⁺ to the correct position for the major product.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: The C=O carbon is electrophilic because oxygen's higher electronegativity pulls electron density away, creating a δ+ carbon that is attacked by nucleophiles.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap the atom in the carbonyl group that a nucleophile will attack, then draw the attack arrow.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: A Grignard reagent (RMgX) acts as a carbanion nucleophile attacking a carbonyl. The product, after aqueous workup, is an alcohol whose type depends on the carbonyl substrate.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Select the correct product of CH₃MgBr reacting with formaldehyde — primary, secondary, or tertiary alcohol?

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: An alcohol attacking a carbonyl under acidic or basic conditions forms a tetrahedral hemiacetal intermediate. A second addition gives the stable acetal (protecting group).
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Draw the two-step mechanism from aldehyde to acetal by placing arrows and intermediates in the correct sequence.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: A base removes an α-hydrogen (adjacent to carbonyl) to generate a resonance-stabilized enolate ion. The carbanion character of the α-carbon makes it nucleophilic.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Tap the α-hydrogen on acetaldehyde that will be removed by NaOH to generate the enolate.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: The enolate (nucleophile) attacks the carbonyl carbon of another molecule (electrophile), forming a β-hydroxy carbonyl compound — the aldol product.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Connect the enolate α-carbon to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon to complete the aldol addition step.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: When heated, the aldol product undergoes dehydration to form a α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound (conjugated enone). This overall sequence is the aldol condensation.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Identify which –OH group is eliminated in the dehydration step and tap it to complete the condensation.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Retrosynthetic analysis works backward from target to starting materials by identifying logical bond disconnections. The double arrow (⟹) means 'can be made from'.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Draw the retrosynthetic double arrow to disconnect the C–C bond in the target alcohol — which bond would you break?

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: A synthon is the idealized fragment from a disconnection, often a carbanion or carbocation. Each synthon must have a real 'synthetic equivalent' (an actual reagent).
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Match each synthon fragment to its correct synthetic equivalent reagent from the list provided.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: FGI transforms a functional group in the target to one that is easier to disconnect. For example, convert an alcohol to a carbonyl before attempting a Grignard disconnection.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Apply FGI to convert the amine in the target molecule to the functional group needed for the retrosynthetic disconnection shown.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Carbon's oxidation state increases with more C–O bonds and decreases with more C–H bonds. Moving from alkane → alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid is progressive oxidation.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Place the four functional groups in order of increasing oxidation state by dragging them into the correct sequence.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: LiAlH₄ reduces all carbonyls (including esters and amides). NaBH₄ is milder and selectively reduces aldehydes and ketones without touching esters or C=C bonds.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Choose the correct reagent (LiAlH₄ or NaBH₄) to selectively reduce only the ketone in a molecule that also contains an ester group.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Ozonolysis cleaves C=C double bonds using O₃ followed by workup. Reductive workup (Zn/H₂O or Me₂S) gives aldehydes/ketones; oxidative workup (H₂O₂) gives carboxylic acids.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Predict both carbonyl fragments produced by ozonolysis of 2-pentene with reductive workup and enter their structures.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Unlike ketones, acyl compounds (esters, acid chlorides) undergo substitution instead of addition because the leaving group can re-form the C=O after the tetrahedral intermediate collapses.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Complete the mechanism of ester hydrolysis by placing the tetrahedral intermediate and the departing alkoxide in the correct sequence.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Reactivity toward nucleophiles: acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide. A better leaving group (weaker conjugate base) means faster substitution.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Rank the four acyl compounds displayed from most to least reactive toward nucleophilic substitution.

tutorial_sequence.short_definition: Fischer esterification is the acid-catalysed condensation of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol to give an ester and water. It is reversible — excess alcohol drives equilibrium.
tutorial_sequence.action_prompt: Identify the leaving group in the Fischer esterification mechanism and tap it to confirm the correct step.
